For everyone looking for work

Life-Changing Work

This site is built to help people find work that changes their life, whether they are starting out, switching fields, or traveling for a better paycheck. Dismukes Recruiting is for everyone — no matter your field, background, or experience — because the right job can help you support yourself, move forward, and build a better life.

Jobs Everywhere: this board is nationwide — employers in any U.S. state can post a job here, and workers can filter the board by state, by Nationwide / Traveling work, or by Remote (U.S.) work. A state filter shows only jobs actually located in that state; states with no jobs yet show an honest empty result until a real employer posts there.

The person behind the board

Meet Destin — The Story Behind Dismukes Recruiting

Destin is a traveling industrial worker who has worked painting and blasting jobs across different states. He knows what travelers actually need — honest pay, per diem that is actually paid, a place to stay, and a fair shot at work — because he has lived that life on the road.

He built Dismukes Recruiting to bring workers and employers together in one place, united, no matter their field, background, or experience — from blasters and doctors to lawyers, drivers, warehouse workers, and first-time job seekers — and to help people find work that can change their life.

Workers apply free. Employers pay to post. Veterans, youth, and people starting over are welcome here.

Why I built this

Destin is a traveling industrial worker who has worked painting and blasting jobs across different states. He built Dismukes Recruiting because he lived what traveling workers go through — getting sent out without clear pay, per diem that was promised but not paid, no place to stay lined up, and employers who never reply. He wanted a site that was different from every other job board: one where workers apply free, pay and per diem are shown honestly, veterans, youth, first-time workers, and people without stable housing are welcome, and employers are held to what they actually posted. One place, united, for blasters, doctors, lawyers, drivers, warehouse workers, and everyone else — work that can change a life, not just fill a shift.

Family history

The Dismukes name

The Dismukes name carries a hard-work heritage. In the data shown in the chart below — covering 1945 to 2004 in the United States — Dismukes life expectancy was at its lowest in 1945, at 40, and stood at 72 in 2004, per the Social Security Death Index (SSDI) as shown in that image.

As the image itself notes, an unusually short lifespan in that data may indicate that ancestors lived in harsh conditions. That history is part of why honest, life-changing work matters here: work that helps people support themselves and move forward.

Before you travel for any job

Worker Bill of Rights

Simple, plain-language expectations every worker should ask for before traveling for a job. If an employer won't put these in writing, that's worth knowing before you spend money getting there.

1

Pay in writing

Ask for your hourly pay — and how overtime works — in writing before you travel, not just over the phone.

2

Per diem in writing

Ask for the per diem amount, how many days it covers, and when it is paid — in writing.

3

Start date

Ask for the actual start date, and what day and time to show up.

4

Job site address

Ask for the full job site address, so you can plan travel, lodging, and your drive before you leave.

5

Contact person

Ask for the name and phone number of the person to contact when you arrive — and if anything goes wrong.

6

First paycheck date

Ask when your first paycheck lands, so you can plan food, fuel, and lodging until then.

Please read this part: this list is general guidance only — it is not legal advice, and it does not create any legal right. Dismukes Recruiting does not enforce employer promises. Each employer sets its own pay, per diem, and terms, and the employer's own posting and paperwork control. Use the Before You Travel Checklist to tick these off before you go.

Veterans, transitioning service members & military spouses

Veterans Welcome

Veterans, transitioning service members, and military spouses are welcome here. Your service, training, and experience matter — bring them. On the worker sign-up form you can mark that you are a veteran, transitioning service member, or military spouse and list the military skills you want to translate to civilian work. Worker applications are free for everyone — including veterans. Use the board's “Veteran-Friendly Jobs” filter to see only jobs an employer has actually marked veteran-friendly.

Veteran resources

These are outside organizations listed as resources only — Dismukes Recruiting does not claim any endorsement or partnership with them, and listing them is not a guarantee of a job. Check your eligibility with each organization directly.

VA Transition Assistance Program (TAP)

Official VA transition support for service members moving to civilian life, including employment assistance, financial planning, and benefits navigation. Find it at va.gov.

VA Veteran Readiness and Employment (VR&E)

One-on-one counseling, training, and employment support for eligible veterans with service-connected disabilities. Learn more at va.gov/careers-employment.

U.S. Department of Labor — VETS

The Veterans' Employment and Training Service (VETS) at the U.S. Department of Labor offers job training, resume assistance, and employment programs for veterans.

Hire Heroes USA

Free, personalized career services for transitioning service members, veterans, and military spouses — including one-on-one career coaching, resume help, and interview preparation — at no cost to the job seeker, at hireheroesusa.org.

USAJOBS

The federal jobs board. Veterans can narrow their search by the Veterans hiring path to find federal openings set up for veterans.

Veterans Crisis Line

Free, confidential support, 24/7. In the U.S., call 988 and press 1, or text 838255. If there is immediate danger, call 911.

Verified Veteran — First Look. Something special for veterans who want it: a “Verified Veteran” mark on your worker profile, earned only after Dismukes Recruiting reviews proof of veteran status that you send privately by email to dismukesreqag369@gmail.com — for example a VA veteran ID card, a veteran designation on your driver's license, or a REDACTED DD214. Self-reported veteran status alone does not earn this mark.

Protect yourself: do NOT send an unredacted DD214, and do NOT send any document showing your Social Security number — black out your Social Security number, date of birth, and other sensitive details first. Do NOT post proof publicly anywhere on this site. Proof goes only to Dismukes Recruiting by email for review, and it is not published.

The benefit is priority, only: Verified Veteran profiles appear first in the employer resume database search — the “First Look” group — and Verified Veterans get the first job-alert email when a new job in their field posts, before the general weekly list. No job is promised, no employer hiring preference is promised, and there is no discount — employers still make their own hiring decisions.

Email Proof for Review (Redacted Only)

For workers — day one, handled

First-Day Checklist — What to Bring

Got the job? Here's a simple general checklist of what to bring on day one, so you show up ready instead of scrambling.

Pack these the night before

Work through this list before your first shift:

  • Photo ID — a government-issued ID, plus anything else the employer asked you to bring for hiring paperwork.
  • Your certifications — the actual cards or copies for every cert the posting requires or that you listed when you applied (for example OSHA 10, C7, C12, TWIC, BLS).
  • PPE — the personal protective equipment the posting or employer says to bring: hard hat, safety glasses, gloves, hearing protection, respirator, or harness, as required for that job.
  • Work boots — sturdy work boots; safety-toe (steel or composite) if the posting requires them.
  • Lunch — food for your shift, especially on sites where leaving for lunch isn't practical.
  • Water — plenty of drinking water; outdoor and shipyard work in the heat takes more than you expect.
  • Any tools the posting specifically requires — only what that job's posting or the employer actually lists. If the posting names tools, bring those; if it doesn't, don't buy tools on a guess — ask first.

The posting's own requirements control. This checklist is general guidance only — every job and employer is different. If the posting or the employer lists something that isn't here, bring that too; if you're not sure about anything, ask the employer or the recruiter before day one, not after you arrive.

Before you travel to the site, also check the weather for the job city — see Getting There — and run through the Job Seeker Safety Checklist.

Real roots — skills for life, not just the job

Survival & Self-Sufficiency — Real Roots

For people who want real, back-to-basics skills — for traveling work, outdoor life, emergencies, or living more self-sufficiently over time. This is a map of topics worth learning properly: general education only, not a job promise and not a shortcut.

Shelter Basics

Staying dry and out of the wind matters first. Learn how to pick a safe, legal place to shelter, layer clothing for the weather you actually have, and keep a basic emergency shelter option in your vehicle or go-bag when you travel for work.

Finding & Purifying Water

Carry water with you — never count on finding it. Learn the common ways water is made safer to drink (boiling, proper filters, and purification products used exactly as directed) and why untreated outdoor water is never assumed safe.

Fire Safety & Fire-Starting Basics

Fire is a tool and a hazard at the same time. Learn fire safety first: only where fires are legal and allowed, in a proper fire ring or stove, cleared of brush, never left unattended, and fully put out. Practice basic fire-starting with matches or a lighter in safe conditions — never during dry, windy weather or burn bans.

Food Basics — Growing, Storing, Fishing & Hunting

Growing some of your own food, storing staples safely so they keep, and knowing where your food comes from are skills that pay off anywhere. Fishing and hunting only where legal, in season, and with the proper license — check your state and local rules first, every time.

First Aid Basics

Every worker and traveler should know basic first aid: how to stop bleeding, treat heat illness, and get help fast. Start with the CPR / AED and First Aid courses in Training to Get Hired — lessons there are free — and take a hands-on class where you can.

Staying Safe Outdoors

Check the weather before you go (see Getting There and weather.gov), tell someone where you're going and when you expect to be back, carry water and a phone charger, and turn back when conditions turn bad. Most outdoor trouble starts with skipping one of these.

Straight talk: this section is general information only — it is not professional survival, medical, or legal advice. Learn hands-on skills from a qualified instructor where possible before relying on them. Check local laws and licenses for hunting, fishing, and land use before doing any of it, and never trespass on private land. Keep it respectful and practical: no extreme or dangerous stunts — start small, practice in safe conditions, and know your limits.

How these skills connect to work

Self-sufficiency skills genuinely help in outdoor work, forestry, farming, construction, and general labor — reading weather, handling tools safely, basic first aid, and taking care of yourself on the road make you a steadier hand anywhere. Build on them in Training to Get Hired, then look at the board:

Straight talk: no survival jobs are invented here, and no job on this board is claimed to require survival skills unless its own posting actually says so. These skills alone do not promise anyone a job, and they do not by themselves let someone live off-grid — they are life skills that support the work, not a guarantee.

No permanent address? You're still welcome here

No Home? You Can Still Apply

Plainly: you do not need a permanent home address to look at jobs here. Browsing is free and open to everyone. To sign up and apply, the crew list form asks for your name and a cell phone number — an email address helps but is not required, and for “home base” a city or area is enough to start getting matched. Each employer sets its own requirements, and the posting controls — some jobs may ask for more, and that will be in the posting or come from the employer.

Dial 2-1-1 — United Way 211

A free, confidential helpline, available 24/7 in many areas, that connects people to local shelter, food, housing, employment, and other services. Dial 2-1-1, or in many areas text your ZIP code to 898-211. Start here — 211 knows what exists near you.

Your Local American Job Center

Free job-search help: computers, resume help, and training funding for eligible workers (see WIOA-funded training in Training). Find yours through 211 or your state workforce agency.

Local Shelter or Day Center

Many shelters and day centers can help with the practical side of starting work — ID, work clothes, bus passes, showers, laundry, and job-search computers. Availability varies by place, so check locally — 211 can point you to the nearest options.

If You Need Help Right Now

If you are in immediate danger, call 911. For crisis support in the U.S., call or text 988 any time. Veterans can call 988 and press 1 for the Veterans Crisis Line.

Honest note: this page does not list a specific shelter, bed availability, or free housing — availability is local and changes day to day, and no housing is promised here. The crew housing some employers provide with a job is different: it appears only on a job card when that employer actually lists it (see the Crew Housing Board). For everything else, 211 and your local Job Center are the real starting points. This section is general guidance only.

Ready when you are: browse the board or join the crew list — free, and no permanent address needed to start.

New to work, or starting over?

Start Here — No Degree Needed

No diploma, no degree, no experience yet? You can still start. This section is a way in: starter fields that commonly hire without a degree, a short brainstorm to help you figure out what to look at, and night school and adult learning options if you want to build skills or finish a credential along the way. Applying and signing up stay free for workers — here and everywhere else on this site.

Starter fields — a way in

These fields commonly hire people without a degree, often training new hands on the job. Tap one to filter the job board above to that field.

General Labor

Site help, cleanup, material handling, and support work — a common first step that can lead toward a trade.

Warehouse & Logistics

Picking, packing, loading, forklifts, and shipping — warehouses hire steadily and promote from the floor.

Hospitality & Food Service

Kitchen, counter, and guest-service work — often hiring fast, with shifts that can fit around school.

Retail & Customer Service

Store and customer-facing roles where showing up reliably and treating people well counts for a lot.

Helper Roles in Skilled Trades

Helper and support roles alongside experienced tradespeople — prep, containment, and crew help are how many painters, blasters, and other tradespeople got their start.

Straight talk on “entry level”: a starter field is a way in — it does not mean every job in that field takes beginners. No specific job on this board is labeled “entry level” here unless its own posting actually says so. Each posting's own requirements control — read the experience, certification, and other requirements on the job card itself before you apply, and when in doubt, join the crew list and ask.

Schedules, class times, and costs change — check the current schedule and cost with the program before enrolling. No prices are listed here because each program sets its own.

Somewhere else?

Check your local adult education program or community college for night classes. Most areas have one — your local school district's adult education office or the nearest community college is the place to ask about GED, diploma, and evening job-skills classes.

Evening Classes at Colleges — and Fast-Track Programs for People in a Hurry

Working during the day? These verified college options run in the evening, online, or on a faster track. Check the current schedule, cost, and eligibility with the college before enrolling — programs, dates, and funding change. And straight talk: fast-track means shorter training — it does not guarantee a job, a credential, or a completion time.

Virginia Peninsula Community College (VPCC) — Workforce Development

Many evening workforce courses are listed 6:00–9:00 p.m., including Tech+, A+, Network+, and Security+ online evening courses in Fall 2026.

FastForward workforce credential funding is limited and first-come, first-served — check eligibility and availability before counting on it.

VPCC also runs “Fast Track” enroll-in-a-day events (listed 2:00–5:00 p.m. at the Hampton and Historic Triangle campuses), where you can meet Admissions, Advising, and Financial Aid at once and get enrolled. Check vpcc.edu for current Fast Track dates, schedules, and costs.

Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College (MGCCC) — Harrison County Campus

A new evening Electrical Technology program, Monday–Thursday 5:30–9:30 p.m., built for working adults and career changers, with pathways into apprenticeships through the Mississippi Construction Education Foundation.

MGCCC also offers a ten-month accelerated Electrical Technology program, and fast-track Defense Industry Training Accelerated Courses (DITAC) in advanced manufacturing, shipbuilding, and defense technologies, designed to shorten training time.

Scholarships may be available through the college's trades programs — check mgccc.edu for current amounts, eligibility, schedules, and costs.

Somewhere else?

Community colleges in most areas offer evening, online, and accelerated options. If your city isn't listed here, search your local community college for “evening” and “fast-track” or “accelerated” programs — that's the fastest way to find what's actually offered near you.

Young people & first-time workers

Youth & First Jobs

Thank you for starting your work journey here. If you are a young person or this would be your very first job — welcome. You don't need a long work history to begin: browse the starter fields below, read the first-job guide, and apply free like everyone else on this site. Applying and signing up stay free for workers, including young and first-time workers.

Starter fields that commonly hire first-time workers

These fields commonly hire first-time workers, often training new hands on the job. Tap one to filter the job board to that field.

General Labor

Site help, cleanup, and support work — a common first job and a way to learn how a job site runs.

Warehouse

Picking, packing, and loading in Warehouse & Logistics — steady work that teaches reliability and teamwork.

Hospitality

Kitchen, counter, and guest-service work in Hospitality & Food Service — often a first job with shifts around school.

Retail

Store roles in Retail & Customer Service where showing up on time and treating people well counts for a lot.

Customer Service

Helping customers in person, by phone, or online — also under Retail & Customer Service on this board.

Straight talk on age and requirements: a starter field does not mean every job in it hires young or first-time workers. Each employer sets its own minimum age and requirements, and the posting controls — read the age, experience, and other requirements on the job card itself before you apply. No specific job on this board is labeled youth-friendly unless its own posting actually says so. Workers under 18 should check with a parent or guardian and with the employer about age, hours, and permission rules before applying or starting. This section is general guidance only — it is not legal advice.

First-job guide

1

How to apply

Pick a job on the board and tap Apply, or join the crew list in For Workers — both are free. Fill in your name, phone, and field honestly; no experience yet is okay to say. Never pay anyone to apply.

2

What to bring to an interview

Bring a photo ID if you have one, a way for the employer to reach you, and any papers the employer asked for. Ask the employer ahead of time exactly what they need — requirements are theirs, not this site's. Dress clean and neat, and bring a pen.

3

Showing up on time

Plan to arrive early, every shift. Set out your clothes and ride the night before, set an alarm, and if something goes wrong, call ahead — employers remember who shows up and who communicates.

For traveling workers

Where You'll Stay & What It Costs

Traveling for work means finding a place to land before you ever see the jobsite. Here is a plain snapshot of the two main job locations on this board, so you can picture the place — and the cost — before you apply. All prices are approximate guides from October 2026, not quotes. Rents and lodging rates move; check current prices before you book or commit to anything.

Newport News, VA

A shipyard city on the Virginia coast in Hampton Roads, with shipyard, waterfront, and suburban neighborhoods nearby — most of the board's shipyard, healthcare, and legal openings sit here or close by.

Average apartment rent: about $1,465/month

  • Studio: about $1,066/month
  • 1-bedroom: about $1,322/month
  • 2-bedroom: about $1,468/month

Rent figures: RentCafe, September 30, 2026 — approximate guides, not quotes.

Extended-stay examples: Extended Stay America, Newport News – Oyster Point, 11708 Jefferson Ave, and Extended Stay America, Newport News – Yorktown, 200 Cybernetics Way, Yorktown, VA. Recent weekly standard rates ran roughly $490–$610 for a studio / 1-bedroom suite, with weekly discounts for stays of 7 nights or more.

Lodging types travelers here commonly use:

  • Extended-stay hotel — kitchenette, weekly rates, no lease
  • Short-term rental — a room or whole place booked by the week or month
  • Shared crew housing — splitting a rental with other hands on the same job

Check current lodging: search “extended stay Newport News, VA” on a booking site before committing — rates change week to week.

Getting There — Flights, Buses & Rides

Found a job in another city? Check what it actually costs to get there before you accept. Use the fare and ride tools below: enter your home city and the job city on that site or app, pick your dates, and check the current fare or ride cost there.

Straight talk: Dismukes Recruiting does NOT sell flights or bus tickets, does NOT book rides, and does NOT set fares or ride prices. No flight price, bus price, ride price, route, schedule, driver, or availability is listed on this page — fares and ride costs change constantly and must be checked on the booking site or in the ride app itself. If a route is not served, the booking site will show that. The tools below are outside booking/search sites and ride apps listed by name only; Dismukes Recruiting does not claim a partnership with them.

Before you travel — check the weather for the job city. Enter the job city and state in the National Weather Service forecast at weather.gov and look at conditions for your travel day and your first days on site, so you don't drive or fly to a job site in severe weather unaware. Check before you leave and again the morning you travel.

Practical tips for traveling workers

Life Hacks for Workers on the Road

Small, practical habits that make travel work cheaper, safer, and less stressful. These are everyday tips only — no promises attached to any of them.

Save Money on the Road

Cook simple meals where you can — an extended-stay kitchenette or a cooler and a hot plate (where allowed) beats eating out every shift. Share lodging with a trusted crew member when you're both comfortable with it. And track per diem vs. what you actually spend with the Paycheck Math calculator and the Can I Afford to Take This Job? calculator, so the money picture is real before you commit.

Stay Ready for Work

Keep a go-bag packed: ID, certification cards, PPE, work boots, work clothes, and a phone charger — the First-Day Checklist is your packing list. Keep copies of your certs on your phone (clear photos of the front and back), so a lost wallet never costs you a start date.

Stay Connected & Safe

Charge your phone every night and carry the charger — your phone is your job line, your map, and your bank. Tell someone your job location and when you expect to check in. Check the weather and your travel route before you leave — see Getting There and weather.gov — so a storm or a closed road never surprises you mid-trip.

Keep Your Papers Straight

Keep one folder — paper or on your phone — for pay stubs, per diem records, and your anonymous pay notes for Verified Pay Check. If pay ever doesn't match the listing, you'll have the dates and numbers in front of you.

Straight talk: these are general practical tips only — not financial advice and not medical advice, and none of them promises savings, a job, or any outcome. Skip anything that doesn't fit your situation, and never take an unsafe shortcut to save money or time — no tip here is worth an injury.

Do it yourself — general information only

DIYs — Hands-On Basics

Work and home projects that fit the trades on this board — the kind of hands-on practice that builds real skill over time. General information only: start simple, work safely, and know where the line is between a DIY project and a licensed professional's job.

Basic Tool Care

Clean tools after use, dry them before storing, keep metal parts lightly oiled against rust, and keep blades and bits sharp or replaced. Inspect cords, plugs, and guards before every use — a damaged tool gets repaired or retired, not “made to work.” Safety: unplug or remove the battery before cleaning or adjusting any power tool, and follow the manufacturer's instructions for your exact tool.

Painting Prep Basics

Most of a good paint job is prep: clean the surface, scrape what's loose, sand rough spots smooth, patch small holes and let filler dry fully, tape and mask what's staying clean, and prime bare or stained spots before the finish coat. Safety: wear a proper mask or respirator, gloves, and eye protection; keep air moving; and treat old paint in older buildings with care — if you suspect lead paint, stop and get it checked before sanding.

Simple Home Repairs

Starter-level fixes: patching a small drywall hole, replacing a toilet flapper to stop a running toilet, clearing a slow drain with a plunger, and tightening loose hinges and handles. Safety: turn off the water or power to whatever you're working on where relevant, and if a “simple” repair turns out bigger than it looked, stop and ask a qualified person.

Simple Storage & Work Organizers

Build a basic shelf, a tool tote, or a parts organizer from measured lumber or plywood: measure twice, mark your cuts, clamp the work, and keep cuts simple and straight. Safety: eye protection on for every cut, follow the saw manufacturer's instructions, and keep hands clear of the blade path — always.

Safety, on every project: wear the PPE the job calls for, follow the tool manufacturer's instructions, turn off power or water where relevant, and stop and ask a qualified person if you are unsure — that is a skill, not a failure. Licensed work stays licensed: these guides do not cover doing electrical, gas, structural, or other work that requires a license yourself — for that work, hire a licensed professional.

For night shifts, travelers & night-sky people

Stars & Moon

Night-shift hands, travelers sleeping in new towns, and anyone who loves the night sky: this corner of the site is for you. The people who work while the world sleeps often see the sky everybody else misses — this section is for rest and wonder on your off hours. It is free, it is not a job requirement, and nothing here promises clear skies.

Tonight's moon

Working out tonight's phase from today's date…

Find a Dark Spot

When you're off shift and it's safe to do so, get away from city lights, yard lights, and headlights — a quiet spot outside town or a dark corner of a rest area shows far more sky than a lit-up parking lot. Stay somewhere safe and legal, and never trespass.

Let Your Eyes Adjust — About 20 Minutes

Your eyes need roughly 20 minutes in the dark before they really open up. Put the phone away for a while — one glance at a bright screen restarts the clock — and the stars will keep getting clearer.

Look Up on a Clear Night

Start simple: find the Moon, pick out the brightest stars, and follow the Milky Way when the night is dark enough. No gear needed — binoculars help if you have them, but your eyes are enough to start.

Want Names for What You See?

A free star-chart app on your phone can name the stars and planets overhead — point it at the sky and explore. No app is endorsed here and none is a partner of Dismukes Recruiting; pick any free one you like.

Straight talk about the moon above: the phase is computed from today's date in your own browser, the same way a moon-phase calculator works — cycling through new, crescent, quarter, gibbous, full, and back over about 29.5 days. It is a date-computed estimate only — not a live telescope feed and not live sky data. And no star, planet, or event is promised to be visible on any given night: clouds, light, and where you are decide that. This section is for rest and wonder — never a job requirement, and no clear skies are promised.

Paycheck Math Calculator

Want a rough idea of what a week could add up to before you take a job? Enter the hours, the hourly rate, and any per diem from the job listing — this calculator does the simple math for one week.

Before-tax estimate only. This is simple math — hours × rate, plus per diem × days. Taxes, deductions, and fees are not included, so your actual take-home pay will be different. The employer makes the final pay decision, and this estimate is not a promise of take-home pay or of any job.

For workers — run the real numbers

Can I Afford to Take This Job?

A paycheck only tells half the story when you're traveling — lodging eats the rest. Enter the pay from the job listing and what a week of rent or lodging would cost you there, and see what's left over for the week. Check your flight or bus fare first in Getting There — Flights, Buses & Rides and your lodging in Where You'll Stay, so travel cost, lodging cost, and pay are all in front of you before you accept.

Before-tax estimate only. This is pay + per diem, minus the lodging figure you entered. Taxes, food, fuel, and other costs are not included, so what you actually keep will be less. The employer makes the final pay decision, and this is not a promise of take-home pay.

Protect yourself

Job Seeker Safety Checklist

Real employers don't charge workers to hire them. Run through this short list before you apply, pay for anything, or travel anywhere for a job.

  • Never pay an employer to apply for a job. Applying here is always free for workers — and a “fee to apply” anywhere is a warning sign.
  • Never send money, gift cards, or bank details to get a job. No real hiring process works that way. Don't send account numbers, card numbers, or gift card codes to anyone offering work.
  • Verify the employer before you travel. Check the company name, the job site address, and a real phone number before driving across states — and tell someone where you're going.
  • Keep your documents yours. Don't send ID photos, Social Security numbers, or bank details until you've verified who you're dealing with — and never through a chat app to a stranger.
  • Report a suspicious posting. If a job on this board — or someone claiming to post here — asks you for money or bank details, report it to dismukesreqag369@gmail.com so Dismukes Recruiting can review it.

This checklist is general guidance only — it is not legal advice.

Why Dismukes Recruiting is different

Built different — on purpose

Everything on this list is a feature actually on this site — nothing here is a promise of a job or an outcome:

  • Workers apply free — browsing, applying, and joining the crew list cost workers nothing, in every field.
  • Job Transparency Score — every job card scores how much the posting itself discloses: pay, per diem, hours, location, lodging help, and start date.
  • Verified Pay Check — workers can report whether pay and per diem actually arrived as listed and on time; badges update only after review.
  • Per diem estimator — plus paycheck math and a “Can I Afford This Job?” check, so travelers can see the numbers before they drive.
  • No-Ghosting Pledge — employers can voluntarily pledge to reply to every applicant within 7 days; only those who take it get the badge.
  • Veteran First Look — veterans who send proof for private review appear first for employers and get the first job-alert email in their field.
  • Youth & first jobs — a dedicated section for young people and first-time workers, with starter fields and a first-job guide.
  • Survival & life hacks — real-roots self-sufficiency basics and practical road tips, as general education alongside the job board.
  • Help without stable housing — you can still apply without a permanent address, with 2-1-1 and local resource guidance on the site.

About Dismukes Recruiting

Work for everyone, in every field

Dismukes Recruiting is for everyone looking for work — no matter your field, background, or experience. Whether you are starting out, switching fields, or traveling for a better paycheck, you are welcome here.

The goal is life-changing work: a job that helps you support yourself, move forward, and build a better life. Browse the board, join the crew list, and apply free — and employers can reach workers from all walks of life in one place.

  • Open to all fields, backgrounds, and experience levels
  • Free for workers to browse, apply, and sign up
  • Based in Alabama and Tennessee, recruiting nationwide
Call (251) 422-4242 dismukesreqag369@gmail.com

Straight answers

Questions workers ask

Does it cost me anything to sign up?

No. Workers never pay a fee here. You sign up, and you get called when a project matches your trade, certs, and travel range.

Do I need certifications?

Not for every job — but OSHA 10, C7, and C12 open a lot more doors, and some sites require TWIC or confined-space training. List what you have honestly; experience counts too.

How do pay and per diem work?

Each project sets its own pay and per diem, and the job's location matters here — it affects how far you travel and whether per diem applies. You'll hear both numbers before you commit to anything — no traveling three states on a promise.

What is the Job Transparency Score on each job card?

It's a score out of 6 showing how much that posting itself discloses: whether it states a pay amount, per diem, hours / shift, a specific location, lodging or travel help, and a start date. A posting that discloses more scores higher — no posting scores high unless it actually states those details. It is not a rating of the employer, not a quality rating, and not a promise about the job — it only measures what the posting tells you up front.

What is the No-Ghosting Pledge — and what does “Typical reply time” mean?

Employers can voluntarily pledge to reply to every applicant within 7 days; only employers who actually take the pledge get the “No-Ghosting Pledge” badge on their cards — no employer is badged by default. It is a pledge, not a guarantee, and Dismukes Recruiting does not control employer replies. “Typical reply time” on a card starts at “Not observed yet” for every employer and is filled in only from replies Dismukes Recruiting has actually observed — never guessed, and not a promise.

What should I confirm before I travel for a job?

Use the Before You Travel Checklist: per diem confirmed in writing, lodging confirmed, start date and job site address confirmed, a contact person and phone confirmed, first paycheck date confirmed, and your travel cost planned. It's general guidance only — ticking a box doesn't guarantee anything from the employer, but traveling without those answers is how workers get stranded.

Does location stop me from using this website?

No. This site is open to anyone, anywhere — based in and serving Alabama and Tennessee, and recruiting nationwide. Location only matters for the work itself: travel distance to the jobsite and whether per diem applies.

What happens after I sign up?

Your details go to the recruiter by text or email. Expect a call to talk through your experience, then a call when a matching crew opens. Signing up puts you on the list — it isn't a guarantee of a specific job.

I'm an employer — how do I post a job?

Use Post a Job: Standard is $25, Featured (top of the board) is $50, or take the $99/month subscription for unlimited posts plus resume database access. Fill in the form, pay by Chime Pay Anyone to (251) 422-4242 or dismukesreqag369@gmail.com with your company name and job title in the payment note, and the post goes live after Dismukes Recruiting reviews the payment — paying alone does not post it automatically.

What is the placement fee?

When a worker sent by Dismukes Recruiting actually starts work for an employer, a one-time placement fee applies for that hire. The amount is agreed in writing with the employer before the placement — there is no set figure quoted here, and workers never pay it.

How does the $99/month subscription work?

It covers unlimited job posts plus the ability to search worker sign-ups by field, trade, and location. You pay by Chime Pay Anyone, and access is activated manually after Dismukes Recruiting confirms the payment — it is not automatic, and no recurring card charge is collected on this page.

What is Rush Crew?

On the Request a Crew form, pick Rush Crew to add a one-time $150 rush fee. Dismukes Recruiting then aims to have a crew lined up within 48 hours — that's a target, not a guarantee.

What is the sponsored slot?

One banner at the very top of the job board, rented to a single employer for $75/month, first come, first served. Claim it with the sponsored slot form — it is yours only after availability and payment are confirmed.

I run training courses — can we work together?

Training providers can buy a $30/month listing in the Training section — listing only, not a referral cut — paid by Chime Pay Anyone and activated manually after confirmation (see Training). Providers interested in any other arrangement can email dismukesreqag369@gmail.com. Nothing is in place until it's agreed directly, and no referral income is promised.

What is Verified Pay Check?

Only on this site: after a job, a worker can send an anonymous report to dismukesreqag369@gmail.com saying whether the pay and per diem actually arrived as listed, and whether it was on time. Reports are never published automatically — Dismukes Recruiting reviews each one first, and only then updates that employer's trust badge. Every employer starts at “No confirmations yet.” A badge reflects worker confirmations reviewed by Dismukes Recruiting — it is not a guarantee of future pay.

How do job alerts work?

Pick a field and a location in the Job Alerts section and leave your email. There is no automatic email system yet — alerts are sent manually by Dismukes Recruiting when a new job in your field posts. Free for workers.

How does the per-diem estimator work?

Enter the miles from home to the job site, the per-diem amount listed for that job, and the number of days — the estimator totals the per diem. It is an estimate only: the employer makes the final per-diem decision, because every company sets its own rule.

Are the details on my worker profile verified?

No — your trade, certifications, travel answers, availability date, and per-diem status are worker self-reported. They are not verified by Dismukes Recruiting unless you provide proof, such as a copy of a certification card.

Can the site read the page out loud to me?

Yes. Use the Listen to this page controls at the top of the site, or the Read this job button on any job card. It uses your own browser's built-in text-to-speech — no download, no account, no payment, and nothing is sent anywhere.

What is crew housing, and which jobs offer it?

Some employers provide housing for travelers — a crew house, a hotel, or per diem instead. It appears on a job card and on the Crew Housing Board only when the employer actually lists it on their post. Right now: no crew housing listed yet. Use the “Crew housing listed” filter on the board to check.

Can I save my worker profile for next time?

Yes — in the For Workers section you can save your trade, certifications, travel range, and home base on your own device, in your browser only. It is not sent to Dismukes Recruiting; it just fills the sign-up form faster next time. Nothing is submitted until you submit an application.

What is the Hot Jobs weekly list?

A short weekly email of the best per-diem jobs on the board. Sign up in the Hot Jobs section — the list is written and sent manually by Dismukes Recruiting; there is no automatic email system yet. Free for workers.

What is a “paid on time” streak?

An extension of Verified Pay Check: an employer who earns repeated worker confirmations of on-time pay — each one reviewed by Dismukes Recruiting — can build a “paid on time” streak on their badge. No employer has any confirmations yet, so every badge still shows “No confirmations yet” and no streak.

How do I get a “cert on file” mark?

Email proof of your certification (OSHA 10, C7, C12, BLS, ACLS, etc.) to dismukesreqag369@gmail.com. After Dismukes Recruiting reviews the proof, your profile earns a “cert on file” mark. Until then, your certifications stay labeled self-reported, not verified.

Is the site available in Spanish?

Use the Español / EN button at the top of the page to switch the main headings and job card labels to Spanish. Job details stay in English, exactly as the employer posted them — the employer's posting controls.

What is the Milestone Giveaway?

When 500 people have joined the Hot Jobs weekly list, Dismukes Recruiting will hold a drawing for the winner's choice of a trip to Alaska or a trip to Las Vegas, provided by Dismukes Recruiting. Entry is free — join the Hot Jobs list, or email dismukesreqag369@gmail.com with subject “Giveaway Entry” and your name. No purchase or payment is required. The exact trip details, dates, and value will be announced when the milestone is reached, before the drawing; the winner will be announced on the site and by email. 18+, one entry per person, void where prohibited. Status: entries open — drawing not yet held. See the Giveaway section for the full short rules.

I don't have a degree or experience — where do I start?

See Start Here — No Degree Needed. Starter fields that commonly hire without a degree — General Labor, Warehouse & Logistics, Hospitality & Food Service, Retail & Customer Service, and helper roles in Skilled Trades — are a way in. No specific job is labeled “entry level” unless its own posting says so, and each posting's own requirements control. Applying is free for workers.

What is the Find Your Path quiz?

A short brainstorm in the Start Here section: three questions about working with your hands, people, outdoors, or a computer, traveling or staying local, and day or night work — and it suggests fields to look at. It is a guide to brainstorm only — not a test, not a guarantee of a job, and not career counseling.

Are there evening college classes or fast-track programs?

Yes — the Start Here section now lists them: VPCC Workforce Development evening courses (many 6:00–9:00 p.m., including Tech+, A+, Network+, and Security+ online in Fall 2026), limited first-come FastForward funding, and VPCC “Fast Track” enroll-in-a-day events; plus MGCCC's evening Electrical Technology program at Harrison County Campus (Mon–Thu 5:30–9:30 p.m.), its ten-month accelerated Electrical Technology program, and fast-track DITAC courses. Check current schedules, costs, and eligibility with the college before enrolling — fast-track means shorter training, not a guaranteed job or credential. Anywhere else: search your local community college for “evening” and “fast-track” or “accelerated” programs.

Where can I find night school or adult classes?

The Start Here section lists the verified options: Newport News Public Schools Adult & Continuing Education, Hampton Adult Education, Pascagoula Adult Learning Center, Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College (MGCCC), and Virginia Peninsula Community College (VPCC) Workforce Development, including its Newport News Trades Center. Schedules and costs change — check the current schedule and cost with the program before enrolling. Anywhere else: check your local adult education program or community college for night classes.

How do I share this site with a coworker?

Use the Share Dismukes Recruiting section: tap Share…, or send it by Facebook, WhatsApp, text message, or email. Sharing always happens in your own apps — the site never posts for you and never collects your contacts.

What does the “Starting this week” filter show?

Only jobs whose own posting actually says they hire immediately, offer an immediate start, or start this week. Right now, no job on the board states that, so that filter honestly shows “No same-week starts listed yet” instead of tagging jobs that never said it.

What is the Paycheck Math Calculator?

A simple weekly estimate: hours × hourly rate, plus per diem × days worked. It is a before-tax estimate only — taxes, deductions, and fees are not included, the employer makes the final pay decision, and it is not a promise of take-home pay.

Can I check if a job pays enough after lodging?

Yes — the “Can I Afford to Take This Job?” calculator takes pay + per diem and subtracts your weekly rent/lodging figure to show a weekly leftover estimate. It is a before-tax estimate only: taxes, food, fuel, and other costs are not included, the employer makes the final pay decision, and it is not a promise of take-home pay.

What are Travel Buddies?

An opt-in way for workers heading to the same job site to connect for a carpool or shared housing. Your contact details are shared with another worker only if both of you say yes. Requests go to dismukesreqag369@gmail.com for manual handling — Dismukes Recruiting does not arrange travel or housing, it only passes the request along, and a match is not promised.

Can I add a video intro to my sign-up?

Yes — add a link on the worker sign-up form to a short video of yourself (up to about 30 seconds) that you already posted somewhere else. This site does not host or upload videos. Dismukes Recruiting reviews the link before it is shown, and no video is shown without review.

How do I avoid job scams?

Read the Job Seeker Safety Checklist: never pay an employer to apply, never send money, gift cards, or bank details to get a job, verify the employer before traveling, and report a suspicious posting to dismukesreqag369@gmail.com. It's guidance only, not legal advice.

What does “Ready to Travel Now” mean on the sign-up form?

It's a self-reported marker you can tick if you're available to travel immediately. It is not verified by Dismukes Recruiting — it's only a marker employers can filter by, and it does not promise you a job first.

Can I share my story of getting hired?

Yes — use Fresh Start Stories to email your story to dismukesreqag369@gmail.com. Stories are published only after Dismukes Recruiting reviews them and gets your permission. Right now there are no stories yet — yours could be the first sent in.

Can my whole crew apply together?

Yes — a crew leader can use the Work-Together Crews form to apply as a group: crew size, trades, travel range, and available-from date. Dismukes Recruiting reviews group applications manually and matches crews to employers who need a crew. It does not promise a crew placement, and applying is free.

Is this board only for my state?

No — it is nationwide. Employers in any U.S. state can post, and you can filter the board by state, by Nationwide / Traveling, or by Remote (U.S.). The state filter shows only jobs located in that state, so a state with no located jobs yet honestly shows an empty result until a real employer posts there.

I'm a veteran — what's here for me?

See Veterans Welcome: mark your veteran / transitioning service member / military spouse status on the free worker sign-up (self-reported, not verified), list the military skills you want to translate, use the “Veteran-Friendly Jobs” filter (only jobs an employer actually marked), and check the veteran resources list — VA TAP, VA VR&E, DOL VETS, Hire Heroes USA, USAJOBS, and the Veterans Crisis Line (988, press 1). Check eligibility with each organization; no endorsement or job is guaranteed.

Can I donate to help veterans and special needs job seekers?

Yes — see Donate. Donations are voluntary, you choose the amount, and you send them yourself by Chime Pay Anyone to (251) 422-4242 or dismukesreqag369@gmail.com with the note “Veteran / Special Needs Donation.” Straight talk: donations go directly to Dismukes Recruiting, which is not a nonprofit, so donations are not tax-deductible and do not go to a charity. No card or bank details are collected on this page, no recurring donation is set up, and no specific use or outcome is promised for any one person. Special needs job seekers are welcome here — note any workplace accommodations you need in the worker sign-up form (self-reported); the final accommodation decision is the employer's.

What is the Urgent Hiring Boost?

An employer add-on: $35 keeps a job pinned at the top of the board for 7 days, on top of the $25 Standard or $50 Featured post. Paid by Chime Pay Anyone to (251) 422-4242 or dismukesreqag369@gmail.com and activated manually after Dismukes Recruiting confirms payment — no automatic charge on this page.

Is there a 1-day resume database pass?

Yes — $15 for a 1-day pass to search worker profiles, in addition to the $99/month subscription. Paid by Chime Pay Anyone and activated manually after confirmation — no automatic access on this page. See Employer Extras.

What is the Hot Jobs Top Spot?

An employer pays $20 to be the first job in the weekly Hot Jobs list sent manually by Dismukes Recruiting. Paid by Chime Pay Anyone, activated manually after confirmation.

Can my hotel or training school be listed?

Yes — lodging partners list in Where You'll Stay for $30/month, and training providers list in Training for $30/month (listing only, not a referral cut). Both are paid by Chime Pay Anyone and activated manually. Right now: no lodging partners listed yet and no paid training listings yet — none are invented.

What is Resume Polish?

An optional $25 resume rewrite/polish for workers, handled manually by Dismukes Recruiting after Chime payment is confirmed. Applying for jobs stays free and a polish does not guarantee a job. See Resume Polish.

What is Pay Per Qualified Applicant?

An alternative to paying to post: an employer pays $5 per qualified applicant Dismukes Recruiting actually sends who fits the job, tracked manually. “Qualified” means the applicant meets the posting's stated requirements as reviewed by Dismukes Recruiting. No hiring guarantee.

Is there an annual employer plan?

Yes — $999/year for unlimited posts + resume database access, same as the $99/month subscription, paid a year up front at a discount. Paid by Chime Pay Anyone and activated manually after confirmation.

Can I get a ride to the job site with Uber or Lyft?

See Getting There. Dismukes Recruiting does not book rides and does not set ride prices — check the current ride cost in the Uber or Lyft app for the job city, or contact a local taxi company in that city directly. No ride price, driver, or availability is listed here. Carpool connections through Travel Buddies are opt-in only, and contact is shared only if both workers say yes.

I'm young or looking for my first job — where do I start?

See Youth & First Jobs — thank you for starting your work journey here. Starter fields that commonly hire first-time workers are General Labor, Warehouse, Hospitality, Retail, and Customer Service, plus a first-job guide and training links already on this site (adult ed, VPCC, MGCCC, OSHA 10). Each employer sets its own minimum age and requirements and the posting controls; no job is labeled youth-friendly unless its posting actually says so. Workers under 18 should check with a parent or guardian and the employer about age, hours, and permission rules. General guidance only, not legal advice. Applying stays free.

What is the Travel Info Add-On for employers?

For $10, Dismukes Recruiting manually prepares a flight / bus / lodging travel guide from the job location and adds it to an employer's job posting. Paid by Chime Pay Anyone to (251) 422-4242 or dismukesreqag369@gmail.com and added manually after payment is confirmed — no automatic charge.

What is the Youth Spotlight?

An employer pays $20 to feature a job in Youth & First Jobs for 7 days — only for jobs that actually meet youth-friendly requirements as stated in the posting. Paid by Chime Pay Anyone, activated manually after confirmation.

Can my ride, taxi, hotel, or bus business list in Getting There?

Yes — $30/month for a listing in Getting There, paid by Chime Pay Anyone and activated manually after confirmation. Right now it honestly shows “No Getting There partners listed yet” — no partners are invented.

How do I check flight or bus fares to a job?

See Getting There — Flights, Buses & Rides. Dismukes Recruiting does not sell flights or bus tickets, does not book rides, and does not set fares or ride prices — fares change constantly and must be checked on the booking site itself. Use Google Flights, Skyscanner, or Expedia for flights, and Greyhound or FlixBus for buses, entering your home city and the job city. No price, route, schedule, or availability is listed here; if a route is not served, the booking site will show that.

What is “Verified Veteran — First Look”?

A veteran can earn a “Verified Veteran” mark by sending proof of veteran status privately by email to dismukesreqag369@gmail.com for manual review — a VA veteran ID card, a veteran designation on a driver's license, or a redacted DD214. Never send an unredacted DD214 or anything showing a Social Security number, and never post proof publicly; proof is not published. Self-reported status alone does not earn the mark. The benefit is priority only: Verified Veteran profiles appear first in the employer resume database search, and Verified Veterans get the first job-alert email in their field, before the general weekly list. No job, employer hiring preference, or discount is promised — employers make their own hiring decisions.

I don't have a permanent home address — can I still apply?

Yes — see No Home? You Can Still Apply. You do not need a permanent home address to look at jobs here, and the crew list sign-up asks for your name and a cell phone number (email optional, and a city or area is enough for “home base”). Each employer sets its own requirements and the posting controls. For local shelter, food, housing, and employment services, dial 2-1-1 (United Way 211 — free, confidential, 24/7 in many areas; in many areas you can also text your ZIP code to 898-211), and check your local American Job Center and shelter or day center for help with ID, work clothes, bus passes, showers, laundry, and job-search computers — availability varies by place. If you are in immediate danger, call 911; for crisis support, call or text 988. No specific shelter, bed, or free housing is listed or promised here — availability is local and changes.

What is the Stars & Moon section?

Stars & Moon is a free corner of the site for night-shift workers, travelers, and anyone who loves the night sky. Its moon picture is computed from today's date in your own browser, the way a moon-phase calculator works — it is a date-computed estimate only, not a live telescope feed and not live sky data. The section also shares simple stargazing tips: find a dark spot away from city lights, let your eyes adjust for about 20 minutes, look up on a clear night, and use a free star-chart app if you want names for what you see — no app is endorsed or a partner here. No star, planet, or event is promised visible on any given night, and no clear skies are promised. It is for rest and wonder, never a job requirement.

What is the Survival & Self-Sufficiency section?

Survival & Self-Sufficiency — Real Roots is a general-education section on back-to-basics life skills: shelter basics, finding and purifying water, fire safety and fire-starting basics, food basics (growing, storing, and fishing or hunting only where legal with the proper license), first aid basics, and staying safe outdoors. It is general information only — not professional survival, medical, or legal advice. Learn hands-on skills from a qualified instructor where possible, check local laws and licenses for hunting, fishing, and land use first, and never trespass on private land. The skills can support outdoor work, forestry, farming, construction, and general labor — but no survival jobs are listed, no job is claimed to require them unless its posting says so, and they promise neither a job nor off-grid living.

What are the Life Hacks and DIY sections?

Life Hacks for Workers on the Road collects practical tips — cooking simple meals, sharing lodging with a trusted crew member, tracking per diem against spending with the site's calculators, keeping a go-bag and phone copies of your certs, and checking weather before travel. Tips only: not financial or medical advice, no promises, no unsafe shortcuts. DIYs covers basic tool care, painting prep, simple home repairs, and simple storage builds — general information only, with safety notes on every guide: wear PPE, follow the tool manufacturer's instructions, turn off power or water where relevant, and stop and ask a qualified person if you're unsure. Electrical, gas, structural, and other licensed work is not DIY here — hire a licensed professional for that.

What should I bring on my first day?

See the First-Day Checklist: photo ID, your certifications, PPE, work boots, lunch, water, and any tools the posting specifically requires. The posting's own requirements control — the checklist is general guidance only, so if the posting or employer lists something extra, bring that too.

Can I filter jobs by shift — nights, weekends, rotating?

Yes — use the Nights, Weekends, and Rotating shifts filters on the board. A job is tagged with a shift only when its own posting actually states that shift; shifts are never guessed. Right now no job on the board states a night, weekend, or rotating shift, so those filters honestly show no matches until a posting states one.

What are second-chance jobs?

Employers who are open to hiring people with employment gaps or a record can mark their posting as second-chance on the Post a Job form, and only jobs actually marked that way get the tag and show under the board's Second-Chance Jobs filter. Right now no posting is marked second-chance yet. Marking a job second-chance does not promise a hire — hiring is still the employer's decision.

Where are the apprenticeship and paid training jobs?

In the Apprenticeships & Paid Training section and under the board's “Paid Training / Apprenticeship” filter. A job appears there only when its own posting actually states paid training or an apprenticeship — none are invented. Right now no job on the board states either, so the section honestly shows none listed yet.

How do I check the weather for a job city before traveling?

Use the weather prompt in Getting There: enter the job city and state at weather.gov (the National Weather Service) and check conditions before you leave and again the morning you travel. This site does not provide live weather itself — weather.gov does, and conditions change, so no forecast is posted here.

How does the “Hiring now near me” distance filter work?

In the distance filter on the board, pick the city you're traveling from and enter how many miles you're willing to drive or travel. The board shows jobs whose posting location falls within that range, using approximate straight-line miles between city centers — your actual drive will be longer. Postings with no specific city to measure from — Nationwide / Traveling, Remote (U.S.), or a broad region — are not given a guessed distance and are not counted as within range; the result note names how many couldn't be distance-checked.

How do job fair listings work?

An employer pays $25 per event to list a hiring event / job fair in the Job Fairs & Hiring Events section, with the date, place, and what to bring. Payment is by Chime Pay Anyone to (251) 422-4242 or dismukesreqag369@gmail.com, and the listing is activated manually after Dismukes Recruiting confirms payment — paying alone doesn't post it. Right now the section honestly shows “No job fairs listed yet” — no events, dates, or places are invented.
